structured_output.ground: "Guide us (along) the straight road." Having declared in 1:5 that they serve God alone and seek help from Him alone, the speakers now make their one request. They ask God to guide them on, and along, the road that is straight, level and without deviation. In 1:7 the road is named again, this time by the people who have walked it.

triggers.how: B001 guidance bi-luṭf, B002 heading/sīra, B003 what goes first, B004 gift, B005 offering sent to the sanctuary, B006 bride conveyed to her husband: one root
the road that is the object of the leading

findings.statement: Ihdinā asks to be shown and led along the road, and its root holds one movement across all its branches: something goes forward, gently and in a set direction, toward the one who will receive it.
findings.perceptible: Guidance becomes a single moving act rather than information. It has a direction (hady, the heading), someone or something going ahead (hādī), gentleness (luṭf), and a destination where the one led is received: the gift to a friend, the offering to the House, the bride to her husband. A Turkish reader who hears hidayet only as 'finding the true religion' sees here that the word is about being carried forward.

triggers.how: praise answering a favour (I7)
the favour bestowed, named in the next ayah
affection scene: mercy

findings.statement: While asking to be guided, the speakers use the root of hadiyya, the gentle gift sent to someone held dear, so guidance can also be heard as a gift sent to them.
findings.perceptible: Hidayet and hediye, which Turkish keeps apart, are one root here. The petition then sits between the praise already given (1:2) and the favour named next (1:7, anʿamta): guidance is the gift being asked for, and the thanks for it were given before it arrived.

triggers.how: root ص ر ط B002 and alt س ر ط B001/B002: sarṭ = swallowing; the entry reports that the road is named so 'because the one who goes on it disappears into it as swallowed food disappears'
ḍalla also names going missing, vanishing into something (I1)
sīn variant makes the swallowing root audible

findings.statement: The ṣirāṭ is the road, and through its sister root sarṭ it is also heard as a road that takes its walker in the way a throat takes a morsel, easily and completely.
findings.perceptible: The road becomes active: once the walker is on it, it carries them. With ḍāllīn in 1:7 the surah sets two ways of disappearing side by side, being taken into the road or going missing in the waste. The request is to be swallowed by the right one.

triggers.how: travel.route scene
ṭarīq muʿabbad, the road smoothed by treading (I1)
waymarks along the route (I1)
the road named by those who walked it

findings.statement: Guide us is also 'give us the heading': hady is the set direction, course and manner of going, which the guide keeps on a road that is already laid out.
findings.perceptible: The road is not invented at the moment of asking. It exists, it has marks along it and it has been walked (naʿbudu ~ muʿabbad). What is asked for is the heading on it, and that is why 1:7 can point to the road through the people already on it.

triggers.how: seeking help, directly before (I6)
aʿbada: the mount gives out (I6, minor)
ق و م B009 qiwām, the support that keeps a thing standing

findings.statement: Beside its plain sense of guiding, the root of ihdinā names walking while leaning on two supporters out of weakness (yuhādā bayna ithnayn), so the petition for guidance can also be heard as a petition to be held up while walking.
findings.perceptible: The request becomes bodily. Right after 'from You alone we seek help', the speakers ask to be shown the way and also to be held up on it, like someone who cannot walk alone, while qiwām in mustaqīm names what keeps a thing standing. Guidance is support along the way, not only a pointer to it.

triggers.how: the full entry: al-hādiya/al-hādī is the staff, 'because a man holds it and it guides him: it goes ahead of him'
ق و م B021 ʿayn qāʾima, an eye whose sight is gone while the eyeball remains (weak)
leaning for help

findings.statement: The guide asked for can also be pictured as the hādiya, the staff that goes ahead of its holder, which the holder leans on and follows at the same time.
findings.perceptible: It joins the two senses of hidāya in one object: a staff both goes before the walker and bears their weight. Leading and supporting are one act in the same hand.

triggers.how: pastoral scene: lead animal
herd and fold (I2)
the stray animal (I2)

findings.statement: The hawādī are the leading necks, the front of a herd or of wild game, so being guided can also be heard as a herd following the one that goes first.
findings.perceptible: The 'we' of the petition moves as a group behind what goes ahead. This sets up the danger in 1:7 of being the stray that falls away from the herd.

triggers.how: B005 hady, the animal/wealth sent to the Ḥaram; B006 the bride conveyed to her husband
sanctuary scene: pilgrim / wasm, the brand marking the owned beast (I2)
praise answering a favour

findings.statement: Guide us can also be heard as 'convey us', as the hady is led to the House and the bride is led to her husband: brought to the place where one is received and belongs.
findings.perceptible: It gives the road an end. The one led is not only shown a way but brought in, marked and welcomed, to where they belong.

triggers.how: pace scene: س ر ط B001 the haste of swallowing
pace scene: slowness/ease

findings.statement: Hady is also calm, unhurried bearing, not the rush of one fleeing, so the guided walk can be heard as a composed one even on a road that takes its walker in quickly.
findings.perceptible: It gives the manner of walking: the road carries the walker along, and the walker goes with calm bearing, not in flight.

triggers.how: war.protection: ally
protection pact

findings.statement: Hady is also the man who seeks protection (mustajīr) before he is granted it, so those asking can also be heard as petitioners placing themselves under the protection of the one addressed.
findings.perceptible: It puts the speakers in the position of a client asking for protection, which fits the move from 'we seek help' to 'guide us'.

triggers.how: B002 standing upright, B008 straightness/evenness, B009 qiwām support, B011 erect stature, B012 the upright post/leg: one root
B008 is the straightness of a road

findings.statement: Mustaqīm means straight, and its root is one idea of standing upright, so a straight road is heard as a road that 'stands': level, true and firm under the feet.
findings.perceptible: Turkish 'dosdoğru' and 'doğru' lean toward correct or true. The Arabic keeps a bodily, vertical sense: the same root as kıyam, standing in prayer, and qāma, stature. The road is not bent, and the one who walks it walks upright.

triggers.how: concordance: mustaqīm qualifies the balance (al-qisṭās al-mustaqīm) in 17:35 and 26:182
the Day on which what is owed is settled (I5)
two ways of falling from the road, one on each side
the other side

findings.statement: Beside its sense of straightness, mustaqīm is the word the Quran also uses for a true balance, and its root names the coin of exact weight that does not tip (al-dīnār al-qāʾim), so the straight road can also be heard as one that does not lean toward either side.
findings.perceptible: The road becomes a level beam between two tilts, the two named in 1:7. It also links to the Day of settlement in 1:4, where things are weighed.

triggers.how: sirāṭ/sirāṭī: the sharp sword that goes clean through what it strikes (ص ر ط B003, س ر ط B004)
straightness
war.arms scene: shield

findings.statement: The sirāṭ is also the sword that cuts cleanly through, so the straight road can be heard as a line that goes through without swerving, like a blade through what it strikes.
findings.perceptible: It gives the road an edge and decisiveness. The Turkish reader already pictures 'sırat' as a sharp bridge (kıldan ince, kılıçtan keskin). The Arabic word itself also names a cutting blade, while its plain sense is simply a road.

triggers.how: direct second object, without ilā; concordance: 1:6, 4:68, 48:2, 48:20, 19:43 use the direct form; 3:101, 5:16, 6:87, 6:161, 16:121, 42:52 use ilā

findings.statement: Hadā here takes the road as a direct object, with no 'to' (ilā), so the request can be read as 'lead us to the road' and also as 'lead us along it, on it'.
findings.perceptible: People who already worship and say 'we serve You' are not asking only to arrive at the road. They are asking to be kept moving on it, step after step. This answers the Turkish sense of hidayet as a single conversion.

triggers.how: ṣirāṭa in 1:7 restates al-ṣirāṭ (a substitution, badal) and identifies it by its walkers

findings.statement: The road is definite, 'the road', one already known, and the next ayah names it again as the road of the favoured, so a quality (straight) and a history (walked by the favoured) name the same road.
findings.perceptible: The road is recognised both by its shape and by the people who walked it. The reader should not treat 1:7 as a second, different road.

triggers.how: same istafʿala pattern (nasta-ʿīn / musta-qīm) and the same long-ī rhyme
rhyme in -īm
rhyme in -īn

findings.statement: Mustaqīm echoes nastaʿīn in form and sound, so the straight road of 1:6 answers, in the ear, the help sought in 1:5.
findings.perceptible: The petition is heard as a continuation: the same pattern that sought help (istiʿāna) now describes the road that has 'come to stand straight' (istiqāma).

triggers.how: law.judgment / time: the Day
verdict (I5)

findings.statement: The root of mustaqīm is also the root of qiyāma, the rising of creation to stand before its Lord, so the straight road can be heard as leading toward the Day named in 1:4.
findings.perceptible: It links the road back to the 'Day of dīn' three ayat earlier: travelling upright now looks ahead to standing on that Day.

triggers.how: travel.mount: exhaustion (aʿbada, I6)
B008 walking while held up

findings.statement: The same root names a mount that 'stands' because it is exhausted and can go no further, and still water that has stopped, so beside the uprightness of the road the word also brings to mind the halted traveller who needs to be carried on.
findings.perceptible: It shows the gap between standing as uprightness and standing as having stopped. The petition asks for the first, from people who know the second.

triggers.how: mutawātir reading with sīn
ishmām reading, between ṣ and z; zirāṭ is attested in ص ر ط B001

findings.statement: In the sīn reading the road is sirāṭ, openly the word of swallowing and of a road easily travelled (al-ṭarīq al-mustashal), so the canonical ṣād reading carries that sense beneath it.
findings.perceptible: The reading tradition itself keeps the swallowing and easy-passage sense audible (F3). One word is pronounced three ways, and all three name the same road.

triggers.how: concordance: God is the guiding subject in 109 of 144 uses
direct address continues from 1:5

findings.statement: Hadā is mostly God's act in the Quran, and here the servants ask for it directly, in the imperative of a petition, the form a request to a superior takes.
findings.perceptible: The imperative is not a command. It is the voice of the 'we' who have just said 'You alone', asking for the act the Quran most often reserves for God.

triggers.how: collocate: mustaqīm is ṣirāṭ's leading companion
concordance: 37:23 ṣirāṭ al-jaḥīm; 7:16 a road where Iblīs sits to waylay

findings.statement: In the Quran ṣirāṭ is a road one is guided onto or holds to, and because a ṣirāṭ can also lead to the Fire (37:23) or be sat upon by the ambusher (7:16), the qualifier 'straight' does real work here.
findings.perceptible: Asking for 'the straight road' is not a redundant phrase. Roads in the Quran can lead elsewhere or be waylaid.

triggers.how: body.strength / know.perceiving: hadāʾ, the dull, weak or heavy man

findings.statement: A near form of the root names the dull, weak man, which sets the one who needs leading beside the one who leads.
findings.perceptible: It adds to the image of the weak walker (F5) without changing the plain request.

loaded_words.role: God guides, is asked to guide, or withholds guidance from people; paths and truth accompany the act
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'hidayet' has narrowed to finding or converting to the true religion, a single event. Here people who already worship ask for it as an ongoing act of leading along a road, and the direct-object construction lets it mean 'lead us on it', not only 'bring us to it'.

loaded_words.role: A route presented as the goal of guidance or invitation, or as a course to follow, hold to or be on
loaded_words.departure: Turkish 'sırat' first suggests the bridge over Hell. Here and in almost every Quranic use it is the road of the present life, walked now. A ṣirāṭ can also lead to al-Jaḥīm (37:23), so 'straight' distinguishes it.

loaded_words.role: Qualifies a path or route as straight
loaded_words.departure: Translations give 'doğru', which in Turkish slides toward 'correct or true'. The Arabic stays spatial and bodily (straight, level, upright), and the Quran also uses it for a true balance (17:35, 26:182).

losses.loses: the gentle showing (bi-luṭf), the heading and direction (hady), the one who goes ahead (hādī, the staff), walking held up between supporters, and its kinship with hediye
losses.adds: a religious-conversion sense (becoming Muslim, 'hidayete ermek') that makes it a single event rather than a continuing leading

losses.loses: its audible link to hidayet: Turkish treats them as unrelated words, and the Arabic hadiyya is specifically a gentle gift sent to someone held dear
losses.adds: a general sense of any present, including a formal or obligatory one

losses.loses: the gift and the leaning support
losses.adds: 'ilet' does keep the conveyance sense (bringing someone to a destination), which matches B005/B006; 'göster' keeps only the pointing

losses.loses: the plain meaning 'road', the road that takes its walker in (sarṭ, swallowing), and the ease of passage
losses.adds: the eschatological bridge 'thinner than a hair, sharper than a sword', which pulls the ayah toward the afterlife. The Arabic word does also name a cutting sword (B003), but here its plain sense is a road walked now

losses.loses: the upright, standing body (kıyam, kamet), the true balance that does not tip, and the qiwām that keeps a thing standing
losses.adds: 'doğru' pulls toward 'correct, true, honest'. The spatial 'straight' survives in Turkish, but the moral sense dominates

losses.loses: straightness and evenness: in Turkish istikamet is only 'direction, heading'
losses.adds: a plain sense of direction that, oddly, belongs more to hady (B002, heading) than to istiqāma

losses.loses: the fact that these four familiar words share one root with müstakim: standing up, the rising Day, true value and the people
losses.adds: nothing specific here, but the Turkish reader does not hear the family

grammar: ihdinā is an imperative used as a petition, a request to a superior, not a command; the 'we' carries on from nastaʿīn in 1:5.
hadā takes two direct objects here (us + the road) with no ilā, so the verse can be read as 'lead us to' and also 'lead us along/on' the road; elsewhere the Quran often uses ilā (3:101, 6:87, 42:52).
al-ṣirāṭ is definite (the road already known), and ṣirāṭa in 1:7 restates it by substitution (badal): the same road named by its walkers.
mustaqīm is on the istafʿala pattern of qāma, the same pattern as nastaʿīn: 'having come to stand straight'.
variants: as-sirāṭa (with sīn, mutawātir): brings the root س ر ط, 'to swallow', into the open, together with its gloss 'a road easily travelled, that takes its walker in'.
the ishmām reading (between ṣ and z, mutawātir): one of the three attested pronunciations ṣirāṭ/sirāṭ/zirāṭ of the same road; it adds no new sense but shows that the word was heard in several ways.
structured_output.reread: Having said 'You alone we serve and from You alone we seek help', the speakers ask for one thing: to be led on the road that stands straight. The verb is one root with the gift: guidance is sent gently, like a present to someone held dear, and it is asked for after the praise was given. It also names the staff that goes ahead of the one who holds it and the walk of someone too weak to go alone, held up between two supporters, so being guided means being both shown and held up. The road is an existing one, already smoothed by feet and named in the next ayah by those who walked it. Its name, heard also as sirāṭ, is the road that takes its walker in as a throat takes a morsel, the opposite of going missing in the waste in 1:7. It is mustaqīm: upright and level like a body standing or a balance that does not tip, with room to fall off only on the two sides the next ayah names.
